glossary.definition: The ruling family who took charge of the early Islamic Empire in AD 750 and built the Round City of Baghdad as their capital.
Medieval Islamic Spain and Portugal, famous for lit streets, rich libraries in Córdoba and Toledo, and Granada's Alhambra palace.
A branch of mathematics that uses balanced equations to find unknown numbers, named after al-Khwarizmi's book al-Jabr.
A clear step-by-step set of rules for solving a maths or computer problem, named after Baghdad scholar Muhammad al-Khwarizmi.
Famous ninth-century scholar in Baghdad's House of Wisdom who championed Hindu-Arabic numerals (0 to 9), algebra, and algorithms.
Relating to the early medieval farming kingdoms and small timber towns of Britain between around AD 410 and 1066.
Flowing Islamic decoration made of curling stems, leaves, and flowers weaving smoothly across tiles, carved stone, and metalwork.
A finely engraved brass star instrument held up to tell the time, guide ships at sea, and find the direction of Mecca.
A bustling covered market street, also called a souk, lined with stalls selling silk, spices, carpets, paper, and glassware.
Arabic name for Baghdad's House of Wisdom, the royal library and research academy where scholars translated and tested world science.
A free medieval Islamic teaching hospital with separate clean wards, trained nurses, soothing fountains, and an inspected pharmacy.
The supreme political and religious leader who governed the early Islamic Empire, known as the Caliphate.
Artistic handwriting that turns Arabic verses and wise sayings into balanced, flowing visual art on paper, bowls, and mosques.
A pitch-dark room or box with a tiny pinhole used by Ibn al-Haytham to prove that light travels in straight lines into our eyes.
A walled roadside inn with courtyard wells built every thirty kilometres along the Silk Roads so merchants and camels rested safely.
A wooden Arab sailing ship built from planks stitched with coconut rope and rigged with triangular sails for Indian Ocean voyages.
A trusted pure gold Abbasid coin stamped with neat Arabic script and used by long-distance Silk Road merchants.
A pure silver Islamic coin stamped with Arabic writing that travelled north along river trade routes to Viking Scandinavia and York.
Art built from repeating mathematical shapes such as eight-pointed stars, circles, and polygons drawn with rulers and compasses.
A steamed neighbourhood bathhouse with hot and cool tiled rooms where townspeople washed cleanly with olive-oil soap and rosewater.
Baghdad's world-famous royal library and translation academy expanded by Caliphs Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun.
Arabic for City of Peace, the official name Caliph al-Mansur gave to the circular Round City of Baghdad in AD 762.
Expensive writing sheets scraped from calfskin or sheepskin, used in medieval Europe long after Baghdad switched to cheap rag paper.
A signed paper payment slip from Abbasid bankers that travellers cashed safely in distant cities, giving English our word cheque.
The popular strategy board game played in Baghdad homes with thirty-two carved pieces, which developed into modern chess.
The network of overland desert and mountain trade routes linking China, Central Asia, Persia, Baghdad, and the Mediterranean Sea.
A giant wooden siege catapult using a heavy dropping counterweight to fling stone boulders against city walls in 1258.
A tall rooftop cooling tower, called a badgir, built to scoop fresh outdoor breezes down into shaded Baghdad courtyard homes.

concept_widget.title: Two Worlds Around AD 900: Abbasid Baghdad vs Anglo-Saxon Britain
concept_widget.caption: Tap each lens above to compare everyday urban scale, books, and public life in Baghdad and Anglo-Saxon Britain around AD 900.

eras.headline: World Metropolis vs Small Timber Towns
eras.summary: By AD 900, nearly one million citizens lived in and around Baghdad's brick quarters, while major Anglo-Saxon burhs like London or Winchester held just 5,000 to 10,000 residents.

pillars.status: Nearly 1,000,000 residents across brick quarters and suburbs
5,000 to 10,000 people in leading timber towns like Winchester

eras.headline: Rag-Paper Book Markets vs Rare Calfskin Scrolls
eras.summary: Water-powered rag paper mills supplied over 100 Baghdad bookshops and grand libraries, whereas Anglo-Saxon scribes painstakingly scraped costly calfskin parchment in small monasteries.

pillars.status: Cheap cotton-rag paper, House of Wisdom, and 100+ bookshops
Rare hand-copied calfskin parchment kept inside monasteries

eras.headline: Paved Canal Streets and Bathhouses vs Smoky Muddy Lanes
eras.summary: Baghdad families walked paved streets beside canals, steamed hammam bathhouses, oil lamps, and free bimaristan wards, while most Britons lived along unlit muddy lanes in smoky thatched huts.

pillars.status: Paved streets, canal gardens, bathhouses, lamps, and free wards
Unlit muddy village lanes, open hearths, and thatched timber huts

concept_widget.title: Golden Age Pioneers: Maths, Star Navigation and Hospital Science
concept_widget.caption: Explore how three Golden Age thinkers tested evidence to transform everyday numbers, sea navigation, optics, and hospital care.

items.title: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi

metrics.label: Number Breakthrough
metrics.value: Championed Hindu-Arabic digits 0 to 9 and place-value zero (sifr)

metrics.label: Famous Book
metrics.value: Kitab al-Jabr, using balanced squares to solve unknown numbers

metrics.label: Words We Use Today
metrics.value: Gave English both algebra and algorithm for maths and computers

items.takeaway: Replacing clumsy Roman numerals with 0 to 9 let merchants, builders, and astronomers calculate giant numbers swiftly on paper.

items.title: Mariam al-Asturlabi

metrics.label: Precision Craft
metrics.value: Designed finely engraved brass astrolabes with rotating star plates

metrics.label: How It Worked
metrics.value: Measured the height of the sun or bright stars above the horizon

metrics.label: Everyday Uses
metrics.value: Checked prayer times, steered Indian Ocean dhows, and found Mecca

items.takeaway: Hand-crafted brass astrolabes worked like pocket star computers for sailors crossing wide oceans and travellers crossing deserts.

items.title: Ibn al-Haytham and Chief Doctor Al-Razi

metrics.label: Light Experiment
metrics.value: Ibn al-Haytham's dark pinhole room proved light enters our eyes in straight lines

metrics.label: Hospital Test
metrics.value: Al-Razi hung fresh meat across Baghdad to pick the cleanest air for a hospital

metrics.label: Patient Care
metrics.value: Free bimaristans offered clean wards, pharmacies, and careful bedside notes

items.takeaway: Instead of trusting ancient Greek guesses, Golden Age scientists ran practical experiments that inspired modern cameras and clean hospitals.

source_texts.text: Artefact note: Wide stone steps lead beneath four pointed arches towards an eight-sided shrine in Jerusalem. Notice the blue, turquoise, and gold tiles framing arched windows below the tall curved dome and crescent finial.

Artefact note: Millions of pale tan river-clay bricks form this surviving medieval gatehouse in Baghdad. Trace the long arched causeway on the left, the notched rooftop battlements, and the single shadowed doorway ahead.

Artefact note: Both sides of this thin AD 787 coin shine with yellow gold and carry no ruler's portrait. Count the three neat horizontal rows of raised Arabic lettering framed inside a circular border inscription.

Artefact note: Five lines of bold black Kufic script stretch across this warm tan sheet made from beaten cloth fibres. Spot the red vowel strokes, round golden verse markers, and two blue-trimmed gold margin ornaments.

Artefact note: Inside the painted letter M at top left, two robed doctors compare open medical books beneath red chapter headings. Dense study notes fill the wide right margin of this medieval copy preserving Hunayn's guide.

Artefact note: Drawn in fine black ink beneath three lines of Arabic writing, a turbaned figure kneels with a sword and raised staff. Notice how bright red dots of different sizes mark his shoulders, belt, and foot.

Artefact note: Across this open two-page Arabic manuscript, dark ink lines and red headings explain step-by-step number puzzles. Look at the bottom corners, where neat red-ink squares are split into smaller labelled rectangles.

Artefact note: Six bold black-ink drawings sit directly between lines of Arabic instructions on this medical page. Spot the toothed pincers at the top, the sharp spear-tipped blade, and the curved metal hooks below.

Artefact note: Framed between two leafy trees and neat Arabic recipe lines, a bearded healer in a red tunic sits on a folding stool. Watch him crush herbs in a mortar beside a tripod pot and tall blue jar.

Artefact note: Tiny black stitch marks join the brown wooden hull planks of this tall sailing vessel above three swimming fish. Six turbaned travellers peer from arched cabin windows while barefoot sailors haul ropes and check the mast lookout.

Artefact note: Stamped onto a thin round disc of bright silver, three crisp lines of angular Arabic script fill the centre. Double raised rings and tiny border letters frame the coin right to its rim.

Artefact note: Centuries buried in damp earth left a pearly crust across parts of this small square-sided bottle. Near the base, translucent pale glass and neat cut corners still show below the narrow round neck opening.

Artefact note: Pieced carefully back together by museum conservators, this round Iraqi clay bowl shines with a smooth creamy-white surface. Bold dark cobalt-blue scallops circle the rim around two lines of blue Arabic script inside.

Artefact note: Viewed straight from above, the wide centre of this snowy-white clay bowl holds only one tiny dark dot. Around the sloping sides, tall black Kufic letters stretch inward like spokes on a wheel.

Artefact note: Sixteen glossy turquoise pieces face sixteen dark brown pieces in two battle ranks. Notice the V-notched corner pieces, curved central domes, and small ribbed front markers, all moulded from clay with no faces.

Artefact note: Between lines of Persian chronicle writing, armoured soldiers on the left pull ropes beneath a tall wooden A-frame beam beside stacked round stones. Opposite them, helmeted archers defend high brick walls above tall barred gates.

Artefact note: A high stone-arched bridge crosses the green River Tagus straight into a square crenellated gate tower. Above the river gorge, packed stone buildings and a four-towered fortress crown Toledo's steep rocky hill.

Artefact note: On the left page of this open leather-bound Arabic book, bold black circles map the round eyeball and central pupil. Six pink petal-shaped eye muscles carry neat Arabic labels beside curved black nerve lines.
